A palindrome is a word, phrase, number, or any sequence of characters that reads exactly the same whether you go from left to right (forward) or from right to left (backward). If you reverse it — character by character — you get back the exact same thing you started with.

The clearest examples are individual words. Take the word racecar: spelled out, it's r-a-c-e-c-a-r. Read it backward, it's still r-a-c-e-c-a-r. Other examples include level, madam, noon, civic, kayak, radar, and refer. Even very short words qualify: eye, mom, nun, pop, and wow are all palindromes.

A palindrome is perfectly symmetrical — the left side is a mirror image of the right side. When a palindrome has an odd number of letters, like level (5 letters), the middle character "v" sits at the center as the axis of symmetry, with the letters on both sides mirroring each other (l...l on the outside, e...e just inside it). When it has an even number of letters, like noon (4 letters), the center falls between the two middle letters, and both halves — "no" and "on" — mirror each other perfectly.

Entire sentences can be palindromes too. For a phrase or sentence to qualify, spaces, punctuation marks, and differences in capitalization are all ignored — only the underlying sequence of letters is what matters.

A famous example is "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama." Remove the spaces and punctuation and ignore capitalization, and you get: "amanaplanacanalpanama." Read that backward: "amanaplanacanalpanama." Identical. Other celebrated examples include "Was it a car or a cat I saw?" (stripped: "wasitacaroracatisaw" — same backward), "Never odd or even" (stripped: "neveroddoreven" — same backward), "Madam, I'm Adam" (stripped: "madamimadam" — same backward), and "Do geese see God?" (stripped: "dogeeseseegod" — same backward).

These sentence palindromes are often the result of deliberate wordplay and are considered a kind of linguistic art form.

Numbers can be palindromes too. 121 reversed is 121. 1331 reversed is 1331. 12321 reversed is 12321. Any number whose digit sequence is identical when read in either direction is a numeric palindrome. Even dates can qualify — February 2, 2020, written as 02022020, reads the same forward and backward.

There is a less common usage in which the word — not the letter — is the unit being reversed. In a word-unit palindrome, the sequence of entire words reads the same whether you read the words left to right or right to left. For example, the sentence "Fall leaves as soon as leaves fall" — read the words left to right: "Fall, leaves, as, soon, as, leaves, fall." Read the words right to left: "fall, leaves, as, soon, as, leaves, Fall." The sequence of words is the same in both directions. This type is rarer and more impressive to construct than a simple letter-level palindrome.
What is NOT a palindrome — sharpening the definition by contrast

The word hello reversed is "olleh" — not the same, so not a palindrome. Car reversed is "rac" — not a palindrome. The number 123 reversed is 321 — not a palindrome. The test is straightforward: reverse the sequence letter by letter (or digit by digit), and if the result doesn't match the original exactly, it is not a palindrome.

One important clarification: it is not enough for something to merely sound similar in reverse. A palindrome must be spelled (or written) identically in both directions. The matching has to be exact and literal.
The concept beyond words and numbers

The idea of a palindrome reaches beyond language. In biology, certain DNA sequences that read the same on both strands of the double helix are called palindromic sequences, and they play an important role in genetics. In music, a melody that is structured so it sounds the same played forward or backward can be described as palindromic. In mathematics, palindromic numbers have interesting properties and appear in various number theory problems. The word essentially describes any perfectly reversible, symmetrical sequence in any domain.

No matter what form it takes — word, sentence, number, date, DNA sequence, or anything else — a palindrome obeys exactly one rule: its sequence of elements reads identically from left to right as it does from right to left. That is the whole of it, and everything else about palindromes is simply a variation or application of that one idea.
